featuredProjects.sectionSubtitle: Problem: my notes app was a mess, with unfinished songs, book references and chord progressions scattered around a list. Solution: blend it all together in one structured songwriting app and add AI to play around.

modal.title: VibeComposer
modal.summary: An app for writing song lyrics in Spanish and Catalan with an AI co-writer, a React Flow canvas, a Web Audio sequencer and a mobile version built with Capacitor.

items: Canvas built with React Flow and a sequencer built on Web Audio.
Mobile version wrapped with Capacitor instead of a rewrite.
Supabase backend with per-user row-level security (RLS).
Own pipeline for a word lexicon of hundreds of thousands of words per language.
Rhymes are verified by an SQL query rather than generated by the model.
120 logic tests with Vitest.

items.title: 1. Write
items.caption: Create the song, switch it to Catalan and write the first verse.

items.title: 2. Ask the Muse
items.caption: Select a word and the Muse explains what the verse needs, then suggests a line.

items.title: 3. Rhymes
items.caption: Pick a word, get real rhymes grouped by syllables.

items.title: 4. Chords
items.caption: Long-press a chord and drag it onto a line.

items.title: 5. Voice memos
items.caption: Hum a melody and keep it next to the lyrics.

items.title: 6. Resources
items.caption: Save what inspires you (a phrase, its author, a folder) and find it when you write.

items.title: 7. The whole song
items.caption: Read it through from start to finish, with its chords.

items.title: AI with boundaries to enhance imagination

items: Integrated the Claude API to enhance the writer's inspiration, not to autogenerate songs: the Muse suggests, the writer decides.
API key kept server-side behind an authenticated proxy.
Allowlisted models, capped tokens and per-user rate limits.
Daily quota enforced in Postgres; fails closed.
Rhymes come from SQL, not the model.
Claude API, Supabase, JavaScript and React.

sideProjects.sectionSubtitle: Problem: farmers tend to overuse water, without knowing they can reach an equilibrium: the production they want, with less water. It matters most where water is scarce. Solution: a platform that reads each farm's sensors and satellite imagery and tells the grower how much to irrigate, so the crop gets what it needs and no more.

modal.title: Precision irrigation
modal.summary: A web platform that reads each farm's sensors and satellite imagery and tells the grower how much to irrigate. AI only automates development processes: there is no AI for the user. My work on it is under NDA, so this page shows no screenshots of it.

items: Rebuilt the farmer view: from a legacy scrolling page to a map-centered interface, in the style of Google Maps and Glovo.
Designed for non-technical users in the field: large buttons, generous tap targets and colour only on clickable elements.
Color-coded maps for periodic and on-demand irrigation.
Resolved parcel polygons to the zoom level's point resolution: 57% smaller payload and 22% faster load across 11,160 plots.
Polygon colours update without redrawing geometry.
Built a local-LLM translation pipeline (Ollama, qwen2.5:32b, zero API cost) with a verified glossary: 490 professionally reviewed translations always override the AI.
Localized about 13,000 strings into 6 languages, replacing an estimated 140+ hours of manual work (estimate: about 43,000 words at 300 words per hour).
Adapted one codebase to 10+ regional irrigation authorities, each with its own configuration and terminology.
Automated task creation through the GitLab Issues API.
Built a command that scaffolds every new view.

modal.role: Full Stack Engineer at IRTA (Jan 2026 - present)

columns.heading: My work here is under NDA, so there are no screenshots of it. What the platform does comes from the public sources above, and what I did is explained in words.

items.title: Every plot, on one map
items.caption: Satellite remote sensing of an irrigation district, with each plot coloured by crop. Public image: Canals d'Urgell, via SEGRE.

items.title: A digital twin of each plot

items: Weather data, soil or plant sensors, satellite remote sensing and what the farmer enters about crop, soil and irrigation system.
Every day the new data feeds a digital twin of the irrigated plot, which simulates the crop and its water state.
An irrigation dose updated daily, sent to compatible controllers. The farmer can change the plan at any time.

items.title: From one plot to a territory

items: The same idea covers thousands of plots, using open crop declarations, weather and Earth observation data.
Irrigation communities and public administrations can see each plot and add them up to a whole district or region.
Water demand is predicted up to the end of the irrigation season.

columns.heading: 2. What I did, as Full Stack Engineer at IRTA. AI only automates development: users never see it.

items.title: Visual rework
items.caption: From a long scrolling page to a map-first view, live for paying users.

items.title: Optimization

items.title: Automated translation
items.caption: 13,000 strings into 6 languages with a local LLM. 490 reviewed translations always override it.

items.caption: Automated through the GitLab Issues API.

skills.sectionSubtitle: Problem: small bar owners struggle with the logistics of suppliers, delivery notes, invoices and bank charges, and they can't afford a back office or expensive software to sort it out. Solution: simple tools for the phone that show what is paid, what doesn't add up and what each keg really earns.

modal.title: Estalvia
modal.summary: Tools for small bar owners with logistics problems and no budget for a back office. One reads supplier delivery notes and invoices with AI, shows what is paid and what doesn't add up, and reconciles payments against a CSV bank statement. The other works out what each keg of beer earns. Work in progress: just an idea that still needs iteration.

items: One Django project that mounts each prototype as an app under its own prefix.
Technical decisions and their limits recorded as ADRs.
Invoices and delivery notes read with AI.
The bank statement is processed with rules, not AI.
User accounts with invite-code registration and management commands.
Tests that do not call the model.

items.title: 1. Check the paperwork
items.caption: The photo next to what was read. One tap to confirm, or tap a field to correct it.

items.title: 2. Match the bank
items.caption: Double charges, wrong amounts and payments with no invoice. Nothing counts as paid until a person confirms it.

items.title: 3. Know what a keg earns
items.caption: Profit per pour and per keg, with an alert when the supplier raises the price.

items.title: Small apps can make huge changes

items: Small apps can make a lot of work easier.
Claude reads the documents; a person confirms them.
The bank statement and the keg calculator use no AI.
Amounts must match to the cent.
Work in progress: just an idea that still needs iteration.
Python, Django, PostgreSQL and the Claude API.

expertise.sectionSubtitle: What I bring to a full stack team

skillsList.title: Python, Django & PostgreSQL
skillsList.description: My main backend stack. At IRTA I work on a national-scale precision-irrigation platform, adapting one codebase to 10+ regional irrigation authorities. In Estalvia each tool is its own Django app, every user sees only their own data, and the tests run without calling the model.

skillsList.title: JavaScript & React
skillsList.description: VibeComposer is my full stack proof: React with a React Flow canvas, a Web Audio sequencer, Supabase with per-user row-level security and a mobile build with Capacitor, backed by 120 logic tests. At IRTA I led the frontend refactor from a legacy page to a map-centered interface.

skillsList.title: Applied AI
skillsList.description: I build AI into products with clear limits. In VibeComposer the Claude API sits behind a serverless proxy, so the key never reaches the browser. In Estalvia AI reads documents, but the bank statement goes through rules. At IRTA AI only automates development: I built a local LLM translation pipeline where reviewed translations always override it.

skillsList.title: Performance & real-time
skillsList.description: Two years shipping four commercial Unity titles taught me to measure first. I profiled and fixed severe memory and framerate issues on Android and console hardware, and built a real-time four-player multiplayer mode at a steady 30 fps on mobile. On the web, the same mindset means maps load only the detail the zoom level needs.

skillsList.title: Git & technical decisions
skillsList.description: I record decisions and their limits as ADRs, so I can defend every choice. I work daily with Git and GitLab, and I automated task creation through the GitLab Issues API. Leading a porting department taught me to plan work and advise artists on optimization.

approach.sectionTitle: My approach to the AI revolution
approach.sectionSubtitle: AI writes code fast, and without a process that speed turns into slop. I organize my work with Matt Pocock's skills library.

windows.title: Grilling with docs
windows.description: The agent interviews me before any code. Decisions stay in the repo as a glossary and ADRs.

windows.title: Architecture
windows.description: I decide the shape, the agent works inside it. Deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind small interfaces.

windows.title: Tests
windows.description: One red-green slice at a time, so I check the agent's work instead of trusting it. Estalvia has 121 tests, VibeComposer 120.

windows.title: Clean code
windows.description: Every diff is reviewed against the coding standards and the ticket. In Estalvia, ruff and pytest run in CI.
